occurrenceRemarks: At least two bona fide, old growth Q. douglasii can be found here at the top of a hill directly north of Bouquet Canyon Road near its intersection with David Way. Three other younger trees can be found directly downslope (north) of the largest one, all of which appear to be Q. douglasii, Q. john-tuckeri, or Q. x alvoridana. Overall, at least a dozen separate trees can be found in this small valley and on the hills nearby. All appear to be Q. john-tuckeri, Q. douglasii, and hybrids between them. In the other foothills and hills further away, virtually all oaks appear to be Q. john-tuckeri. While I don't have pictures available, I've driven past this area over multiple seasons, and indeed, both these featured trees appear to be mostly or fully deciduous, which confirms their Q. douglasii heritage. Other trees in this small canyon vary from being fully deciduous to semi-deciduous to fully evergreen.
name: Quercus douglasii Hook. & Arn.

occurrenceRemarks: Mount Diablo State Park Hiked Mitchell Canyon Road and came back via Eagle Peak Trail. This 7.7 mile loop kicked my butt, especially since I went very slow iNatting like a maniac on the way south before realizing how slow I was going... will I ever learn? I decided to complete the loop rather than turning around so I limited my stops on Eagle Peak Trail, which, in any case, was very steep and slippery in some sections and required attention that wouldn't have allowed for noticing as many species. I didn't have trekking poles and was carrying lots of gear so it was rough! Got here by riding BART from Berryessa to 19th ST Oakland before transferring to Yellow line to Concord, then took the 10 bus to Clayton and bicycled to the park entrance. About 2 hours ride each way but no gas emission and only a little slower than a drive here either way! occurrenceRemarks: Flowering Blue Oaks, scattered and growing individually, on dry, grassy, rolling hills in Pinnacles National Park. Blue Oak (Quercus douglasii) Endemic to California. A.k.a. Blue, white, mountain, rock, iron, post, jack, and Douglas Oak. Blue Oak is California's most drought-tolerant deciduous oak and grows 20-60 ft tall. Leaf blade is oblong to obovate. It is adaxially dull and blue-green; abaxially puberulent and pale blue-green. Leaf tip is generally rounded. Margins are +- entire, wavy, or +- lobed. Flora of North America: Acorn diagram: http://floranorthamerica.org/File:FNA03_P83_Quercus_pg_453.jpeg UC Oak Tree Species I.D. and Ecology, University of California: https://oaks.cnr.berkeley.edu/oak-tree-species-id-ecology/ Calflora (with species distribution map in CA) https://www.calflora.org/app/taxon?crn=6990 Oaks of California, B. "Habit: Tree 6--20 m, deciduous; trunk bark checkered into thin scales, +- gray. Leaf: 3--6(8) cm; petiole 3--9 mm; blade oblong to obovate, adaxially dull, blue-green, abaxially puberulent, pale blue-green, tip generally rounded, margin +- entire, wavy, or +- lobed. Fruit: cup 12--20 mm wide, 6--10 mm deep, cup- to bowl-shaped, scales +- tubercled; nut 20--35 mm, ovoid to subcylindric, distally acute to +- obtuse, shell glabrous inside; mature in year 1. Ecology: Dry slopes, interior foothills, woodland; Elevation: < 1590 m. Flowering Time: April--May. Note: Hybridizes with Quercus garryana (Quercus ×eplingii C.H. Harris, 2022 xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx OAKs (genus Quercus) in general: Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family. Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems. occurrenceRemarks: Blue Oak (Quercus douglasii) Endemic to California. A.k.a. Blue, white, mountain, rock, iron, post, jack, and Douglas Oak. Blue Oak is California's most drought-tolerant deciduous oak and grows 20-60 ft tall. Leaf blade is oblong to obovate. It is adaxially dull and blue-green; abaxially puberulent and pale blue-green. Leaf tip is generally rounded. Margins are +- entire, wavy, or +- lobed. Flora of North America: Acorn diagram: http://floranorthamerica.org/File:FNA03_P83_Quercus_pg_453.jpeg UC Oak Tree Species I.D. and Ecology, University of California: https://oaks.cnr.berkeley.edu/oak-tree-species-id-ecology/ Calflora (with species distribution map in CA) https://www.calflora.org/app/taxon?crn=6990 Oaks of California, B. Pavlik, P. Muick, S. Johnson, M. Popper, 1991, pp. 46, 16-18. Blue Oak (Quercus douglasii), Jepson eFlora: https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=40581 Native. "Habit: Tree 6--20 m, deciduous; trunk bark checkered into thin scales, +- gray. Leaf: 3--6(8) cm; petiole 3--9 mm; blade oblong to obovate, adaxially dull, blue-green, abaxially puberulent, pale blue-green, tip generally rounded, margin +- entire, wavy, or +- lobed. Fruit: cup 12--20 mm wide, 6--10 mm deep, cup- to bowl-shaped, scales +- tubercled; nut 20--35 mm, ovoid to subcylindric, distally acute to +- obtuse, shell glabrous inside; mature in year 1. Ecology: Dry slopes, interior foothills, woodland; Elevation: < 1590 m. Flowering Time: April--May. Note: Hybridizes with Quercus garryana (Quercus ×eplingii C.H. Mull.), Quercus john-tuckeri (Quercus ×alvordiana), Quercus lobata (Quercus ×jolonensis Sarg.)." Jepson eFlora https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=40581 Leaf Terminology: Simple Diagrams/Definitions: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e8/Leaf_morphology.svg Plant Identification Terminology: An Illustrated Glossary, 2nd ed., by James Harris and M. Harris, 2022 xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx OAKs (genus Quercus) in general: Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family. Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems. occurrenceRemarks: OK, so the story behind this weirdly shaped Blue Oak tree is as follows: 1) first there was a fertile acorn; 2) many years later, the Oak tree was partially blown over towards the West, but some of the lateral branches then gave secondary support to the tilted tree; 3) then along came some humans that built the house and an above-ground pool; 4) the second owners built extensive decking around the back of the house and the above-ground pool, and in the process the deck construction crew foolishly sawed off the secondary support branches (last photo); 5) the grandkids grew up and the pool liner got solarized in the HOT Sun and was torn; 6) Ken and Karla bought the house, demolished the pool (got $5.00 for recycled bulk metal), and removed most of the pool decking; and 7) using a wooden joist beam from beneath a portion of the removed decking, we installed a tree support post to slow the Blue Oak tree's "falling down" process ......... Many creatures have used this leaning "Moose Tree" as their home over the years: 1) a Raccoon in 2005 (www.inaturalist.org/observations/91473804); 2) another Raccoon in 2013 (www.inaturalist.org/observations/89029785); 3) an Opossum in 2015 (www.inaturalist.org/observations/89028883); 4) numerous birds, including Starlings in 2008 (www.inaturalist.org/observations/117782494) and White-breasted Nuthatches in 2009 (www.inaturalist.org/observations/117783711); and 5) numerous Fox Squirrels (www.inaturalist.org/observations/94772165 in 2008) and (www.inaturalist.org/observations/161139244 in 2023). The Big Question nowadays is "Which way will the Oak tree begin to lean towards", and I hope that we never have to cut it down ......... the "Moose Tree" has so much character and it has given us so much enjoyment .......... and tons and tons of Acorns .......... P.S. I think that it looks more like a Reindeer rather than a Moose, but who knows ........
